Write chapter 8 of the book, `docs/book/08-builtin-math.md`, following the [book guide](book-guide.md) and its phase chapter template.

Source prompt: [gdjl-05-builtin-math](../gdjl-05-builtin-math.prompt.md).

## Focus

- **Porting as a well-posed task.** "Port every public member of the corresponding C# file" with an attribution comment gives a complete checklist and licensing hygiene (MIT).
- **The engine as the oracle.** Golden tests generated by running the same expressions in Godot (GDScript cases → `scripts/make_math_golden.jl` → fixtures). The agent cannot fool itself, because the expected values come from the reference.
- **Explicit scope fences.** "Swizzle-free: C# has no swizzling; do not add it." Show how a single sentence prevents a typical case of AI scope creep.
- **Hand-written vs generated.** Why these types are hand-written while their layouts are generated (ADR 0005).
- **`${input:types:all types}`.** Lets the work be split into smaller sessions.

## Leads to Verify

- `Basis` stores memory rows (`row0..row2`) with an inner constructor `Basis(Internals.ROWS, r0, r1, r2)`, while `Basis(x, y, z)` takes columns. This is a classic convention trap; check how the tests caught or prevent it.
- Godot 4.7 `Projection` uses closed forms (`get_z_near/far`, `get_fov`, `get_lod_multiplier = 2/c00`). The lesson was to fetch `core/math/*.cpp` at the pinned tag instead of trusting model memory.
- `Mathf.EPSILON` uses the engine's `CMP_EPSILON` (ADR 0005).
- Every operation is allocation-free, with allocation tests.
